correct_citation: Weinstein, M., Whitesell, E. R., & Schwartz, A. E. (2013). Museums, Zoos, and Gardens: How Formal-Informal Partnerships Can Impact Urban Students' Performance. IESP Working Paper #04-13. NYU Institute for Education and Social Policy. ERIC ED556797.
design: Student-level fixed effects models with year and school effects, student controls and an indicator for performance in the year before joining UA; linear probability models for long-term outcomes; ELA/math falsification test
population_location: New York City public middle school students (grade 8)
outcome: NYS Intermediate Level Science exam (grade 8); taking and passing Living Environment and Earth Science Regents in grade 8 or 9; attending a STEM high school
effect_as_reported: At least 0.041 SD (0.05-0.06 SD) on the ILS exam; small positive effect on passing a science Regents (Living Environment, Earth Science); null or slightly negative on taking a Regents and attending a STEM high school
excerpt: Results from the fixed effects models show that, on average, UA students do at least 0.041 standard deviations better than students at non-UA schools on the Intermediate Level Science (ILS) exam.
note: Regents passing result described as "some evidence" / "may"; no effect on ELA and math (falsification test).

correct_citation: Weinstein, M. G., & Shiferaw, M. (2017). The Urban Advantage: The impact of informal science collaborations on student achievement. New York University Steinhardt. WWC review of study 86087 (August 2018).
design: Quasi-experimental design; meets WWC standards with reservations (baseline equivalence satisfied)
population_location: 223,775 students grades 6-8 in 514 NYC public middle schools; analysis sample 199,603
outcome: NYS Intermediate Level Science (ILS) exam, 8th grade
effect_as_reported: Statistically significant positive; WWC improvement index +2 (no g shown on page); evidence tier 2
excerpt: Rating: Meets WWC standards with reservations because it uses a quasi-experimental design in which the analytic intervention and comparison groups satisfy the baseline equivalence requirement.
note: Rating, design, outcome and favorable significant direction confirmed. g = 0.06 not displayed on the WWC page (improvement index +2 is consistent with g about 0.05). Components listed by WWC: intensive PD, classroom materials, free access to institutions for class trips and independent visits; "family visit vouchers" not named. WWC page is secondary to the 2017 report, which was not fetched.

correct_citation: Whitesell, E. R. (2016). A day at the museum: The impact of field trips on middle school science achievement. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 53(7). doi:10.1002/tea.21322. ERIC EJ1109830.
design: Six years of student-level data; school fixed effects exploiting within-school variation in field-trip participation over time
population_location: New York City middle school students
outcome: NYS standardized eighth-grade science exam scores and proficiency
effect_as_reported: Small positive effects; largest for Hispanic and free/reduced-price lunch students; magnitude not available
excerpt: Using a rigorous identification strategy with school fixed effects to capitalize on variation in field trip participation within schools over time, I found small positive effects of exposure to field trips on students' science test scores and proficiency.
note: Design, population, outcome, direction and subgroup pattern confirmed from the ERIC abstract. Full text (Wiley) was blocked, so the effect size could not be confirmed.

correct_citation: Holian, L., Warner-Griffin, C., & Gold, B. P. (2024). Gear Up 4 STEM: Final Impact Report. Technical report for Knox County Schools. ERIC ED648513.
design: Quasi-experimental; comparison students from the same schools via propensity score stratification or coarsened exact matching; baseline equivalence assessed (all standardized differences <= 0.25, those 0.05-0.25 included as covariates)
population_location: Grades 3-5, Knox County Schools, Tennessee; STEM camp during school breaks
outcome: TNReady science scale score; school attendance rate (intervention and follow-up years)
effect_as_reported: Intervention-year science g = 0.11 (p = 0.042); attendance g = 0.04 (p = 0.411) intervention year, g = 0.15 (p = 0.066) follow-up; follow-up science g = -0.10 (p = 0.219)
excerpt: Students who participated in the Gear Up 4 STEM program had significantly higher scores on the TNReady science assessment in the spring of the year that they attended the program than a business as usual comparison group.
note: Baseline differences were moderate at most (not all below 0.05), so equivalence was shown with statistical adjustment. Comparison students could attend other afterschool programs.

correct_citation: Snyder, C., & Stevenson, O. (2021). G2ROW STEM: Girls and Guys Realizing Opportunities with STEM. i3 development grant evaluation (Grantee Submission). ERIC ED613865; WWC study 90290.
design: QED, matched students in the same grade in the same schools (business-as-usual comparison); WWC: meets standards with reservations
population_location: High-need middle school students in seven Title I Metro Nashville Public Schools, Tennessee; program delivered after school (STEM clubs), monthly Saturday sessions and summer camps, plus mentoring
outcome: TNReady math and science (NCE scores)
effect_as_reported: Treatment gained 7 NCE points more after up to three years (about one-third SD); WWC improvement index: science +13 (one-year, 660 students), math +16 (one-year, 1,084 students), significant
excerpt: Overall, treatment students gained seven NCE score points more than the comparison group students did after up to three years in the G2ROW STEM program. This is roughly equivalent to one-third of a standard deviation.
note: Design, population, delivery (after school, Saturday, summer; not school day), rating and three-year follow-up confirmed. The exact g values 0.32 and 0.40 are not printed on the WWC page; improvement indexes +13 and +16 are consistent with them.

correct_citation: Fancsali, C. (2021). Design2Learn: Implementation and Impact Study. Research Alliance for New York City Schools. ERIC ED619410.
design: Randomized controlled trial; 32 afterschool programs randomly assigned to D2L or usual science programming
population_location: New York City middle school students (grades 6-8); ExpandED Schools with New York Hall of Science; 1,125 students in analytic sample
outcome: Science interest and engagement, perseverance, critical thinking (surveys); science grades; in-school (school-day) attendance from DOE records
effect_as_reported: No effect on any outcome; low program dosage (about 32 hours per year)
excerpt: D2L had no effect on students' interest and engagement in science, perseverance, or critical thinking behaviors, as measured by student surveys. It also had no effect on students' academic outcomes (science grades, school attendance).
note: Attendance outcome is in-school attendance from NYC DOE records.

correct_citation: Burt, K. G., Burgermaster, M., D'Alessandro, D., Paul, R., & Stopler, M. (2020). New York City fourth graders who receive a climate change curriculum with hydroponic gardening have higher science achievement scores. Applied Environmental Education and Communication. doi:10.1080/1533015X.2019.1611504. ERIC EJ1274477.
design: Comparison with next-year recipients (n = 993) and matched-school students (n = 1,490); multilevel regression vs first comparison group, then Welch two-sample t-tests
population_location: NYC fourth graders (NY Sun Works recipients n = 638), 2014-15
outcome: New York State Grade 4 Science Assessment
effect_as_reported: Multilevel model: higher but non-significant; t-tests: significantly higher than both comparison groups (p < 0.001)
excerpt: We first applied a multi-level regression model to compare scores between NYSW recipients and the first comparison group, which revealed non-significant but higher scores among NYSW recipients.
note: cite_as omits the journal (Applied Environmental Education and Communication).

correct_citation: Wells, N. M., Myers, B. M., Todd, L. E., et al. (2015). The effects of school gardens on children's science knowledge: A randomized controlled trial of low-income elementary schools. International Journal of Science Education. doi:10.1080/09500693.2015.1112048. ERIC EJ1083156.
design: Cluster RCT: 25 garden schools vs 24 waitlist control schools; general linear mixed models
population_location: Low-income elementary schools in Arkansas, Iowa, Washington and New York; grades 2, 4, 5; n = 3,061
outcome: 7-item questionnaire on nutritional and plant science
effect_as_reported: Treatment gain greater than control, but scores uniformly poor and gains very modest; dose-response with fidelity
excerpt: However, science knowledge scores were uniformly poor and gains were very modest.

correct_citation: Mason, G. R., & Wendt, J. L. (2024). The impact of meaningful watershed environmental experiences on the academic achievement of middle school students. Discover Education. doi:10.1007/s44217-024-00326-0. ERIC EJ1448085.
design: Quantitative ex post facto causal-comparative design; MANOVA
population_location: 1,067 grade 8 students in four middle schools in the Pennsylvania Chesapeake Bay Watershed region
outcome: PSSA ELA, math and science
effect_as_reported: Statistically significant difference in PSSA scores by MWEE participation status
excerpt: The findings demonstrate a statistically significant difference between students' PSSA scores based on students' MWEE participation status.
note: Design, sample, outcomes and finding confirmed from the abstract. "No adjustment for prior achievement" could not be confirmed: full text (Springer) was blocked; the abstract names MANOVA (not MANCOVA) but says nothing about covariates. Direction of the difference is not stated in the abstract.

correct_citation: Robinson, C. D., Chande, R., Burgess, S., & Rogers, T. (2022). Parent engagement interventions are not costless: Opportunity cost and crowd out of parental investment. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 44(1), 170-177 (online 2021). doi:10.3102/01623737211030492. EdWorkingPaper 20-282, ERIC ED671402.
design: Randomized field experiment, stratified randomization of students (1,729 treatment, 1,754 control)
population_location: Five secondary schools (grades 7-11) in England, 2013-14; 5,078 students enrolled; 3,483 randomized; 2,212 completed the survey
outcome: Parent-child science conversations; science unit test scores; other parent engagement behaviors
effect_as_reported: Increased science conversations; no detectable effect on science test scores; decreased other parent engagement behaviors (crowd-out)
excerpt: The intervention increased parent-child at-home conversations about science but did not detectably impact science test scores. However, the intervention decreased parent engagement in other, potentially productive, parent behaviors.
note: Sample size in the claim is WRONG: the study had 3,483 randomized students (2,212 surveyed) in five schools totalling 5,078 students, not about 15,000. England, intervention, null test-score effect and crowd-out are confirmed.

correct_citation: Corcoran, R. P., Cheung, A. C. K., Kim, E., & Xie, C. (2018). Effective universal school-based social and emotional learning programs for improving academic achievement: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 50 years of research. Educational Research Review, 25, 56-72. doi:10.1016/j.edurev.2017.12.001.
note: Citation metadata (authors, title, journal, volume 25, pages 56-72, 2018) confirmed via Crossref. ScienceDirect and the Nottingham repository copy were blocked (Cloudflare); no abstract in Crossref/OpenAlex. Number of studies, science ES +0.19 and the rigour caveat could not be checked.

correct_citation: Zhao, Y., & Sang, B. (2025). The effect of social-emotional learning programs on elementary and middle school students' academic achievement: A meta-analytic review. Behavioral Sciences, 15(11), 1527. doi:10.3390/bs15111527.
design: Meta-analysis of 22 studies (24,510 students, 2011-2021); 76 effect sizes
population_location: Elementary (20 studies) and middle school (2 studies) students
outcome: Overall academic achievement and subject areas
effect_as_reported: Overall g = 0.08; science g = 0.06 (k = 3, SE 0.03, 95% CI 0.01-0.12, p = 0.027, significant)
excerpt: The mean effect sizes for mathematics, English language arts, science, and GPA were 0.08, 0.07, 0.06, and 0.33, respectively. Because the science and GPA outcome data came from only three and six sources, some caution should be exercised
note: Science estimate rests on only three effect sizes.

correct_citation: Checkoway, A., Gamse, B., Velez, M., & Linkow, T. (2013). Evaluation of the Massachusetts Expanded Learning Time (ELT) Initiative: Final Study Findings. SREE conference abstract (Abt Associates). ERIC ED563107.
design: Comparative interrupted time series; 24 ELT schools vs 25 matched comparison schools
population_location: Massachusetts elementary, middle and K-8 schools
outcome: MCAS ELA, math and science (grades 5 and 8)
effect_as_reported: Generally no significant effects on achievement; but 5th grade science significantly higher in the fourth implementation year; no attendance result in this document
excerpt: There were no statistically significant effects of ELT in the first, second, or third years of implementation on student achievement, but in the fourth year of implementation 5th grade ELT students performed significantly higher on science tests
note: Science was not uniformly null: grade 5 science was significantly positive in year 4. The ERIC document is a SREE conference abstract, not the Abt final report, and reports no student attendance result; the attendance part is unconfirmed.

correct_citation: Miller, R. T., Murnane, R. J., & Willett, J. B. (2008). Do teacher absences impact student achievement? Longitudinal evidence from one urban school district. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 30(2), 181-200.
design: Teacher fixed effects plus an instrumental variables strategy
population_location: Fourth-grade students in a large urban district in the northern United States
outcome: Mathematics achievement
effect_as_reported: 10 additional days of teacher absence reduce fourth-grade math achievement by 3.2% of a standard deviation
excerpt: The authors estimate 10 additional days of teacher absence reduce mathematics achievement of fourth-grade students by 3.2% of a standard deviation.

correct_citation: Clotfelter, C. T., Ladd, H. F., & Vigdor, J. L. (2009). Are teacher absences worth worrying about in the United States? Education Finance and Policy, 4(2), 115-149 (NBER WP 13648, 2007).
design: North Carolina administrative data; achievement models with lagged scores and teacher fixed effects
population_location: North Carolina public schools, elementary grades
outcome: Student achievement (math, reading); teacher absences
effect_as_reported: Absences associated with lower elementary achievement (FE: 10 days -> -1.7% SD math, -0.9% SD reading); demand for discretionary absences is price elastic
excerpt: In regression models incorporating teacher fixed effects, absences are associated with lower student achievement in elementary grades. Finally, we present evidence that the demand for discretionary absences is price elastic.
note: Findings confirmed. Design used teacher fixed effects with lagged student scores; student fixed effects were not found in the working paper.

correct_citation: Herrmann, M. A., & Rockoff, J. E. (2012). Worker absence and productivity: Evidence from teaching. Journal of Labor Economics, 30(4), 749-782 (NBER WP 16524, 2010).
design: Detailed data on timing, duration and cause of absences; teacher(-school-grade) fixed effects
population_location: New York City teachers and students
outcome: Student achievement (teacher daily productivity)
effect_as_reported: Loss from a temporary substitute on par with replacing an average teacher with one at the 10th-20th percentile; illness a major cause of absence
excerpt: the expected loss in daily productivity from employing a temporary substitute is on par with replacing a regular worker of average productivity with one at the 10th-20th percentile of productivity.
note: Journal citation confirmed on the NBER page (JOLE, October 2012, pp. 749-782).

correct_citation: Gershenson, S. (2016). Performance standards and employee effort: Evidence from teacher absences. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 35(3), 615-638 (Upjohn WP 15-217, 2015, ERIC ED559216).
design: Difference-in-difference on failing AYP in the first year of NCLB
population_location: North Carolina teachers
outcome: Teacher absences
effect_as_reported: Absences fell about 10 percent; probability of frequent absence also fell (WP: 15+ absences down about 30 percent)
excerpt: Difference-in-difference estimates of the effect of failing AYP in the first year of NCLB on teacher effort in the subsequent year suggest that on average, teacher absences in North Carolina fell by about 10 percent.

correct_citation: Jacob, B. A. (2013). The effect of employment protection on teacher effort. Journal of Labor Economics, 31(4), 727-761. doi:10.1086/669942 (NBER WP 15655, 2010).
design: Difference-in-difference on the 2004 Chicago agreement letting principals dismiss probationary teachers
population_location: Chicago Public Schools teachers
outcome: Annual teacher absences; frequent absences
effect_as_reported: Annual absences down roughly 10%; frequent absences down 25% (published abstract; WP said 20% for 15+ absences)
excerpt: Results suggest that the policy reduced annual teacher absences by roughly 10% and reduced the incidence of frequent absences by 25%.
note: Claim URL (umich EPI page) was blocked by Cloudflare; published abstract fetched via OpenAlex and the DiD design from the NBER WP. Mostly composition effects.

correct_citation: Goldhaber, D., Hansen, M., & Walch, J. (2016). Time to tenure: Does tenure reform affect teacher absence behavior and mobility? CALDER Working Paper 172. ERIC ED573188.
design: Natural experiments with difference-in-difference models on one-year extensions of time to tenure
population_location: North Carolina and Washington State teachers
outcome: Teacher absences; attrition and mobility
effect_as_reported: Absences decreased for probationary teachers under extended tenure laws; mixed evidence on attrition and mobility
excerpt: Across both states we find evidence of decreases in teacher absences for probationary teachers who are subject to the new extended tenure laws
note: Two states (NC and WA).

correct_citation: Rockoff, J. E. (2008). Does mentoring reduce turnover and improve skills of new employees? Evidence from teachers in New York City. NBER Working Paper 13868. ERIC ED501973.
design: Instrumental variables and school fixed effects with non-random mentor assignment
population_location: New teachers in New York City (mentoring program adopted 2004)
outcome: Teacher absences, retention, student achievement
effect_as_reported: Weaker evidence of effects on absences, retention and achievement; retention higher when mentor had worked in the school
excerpt: The most consistent finding is that retention within a particular school is higher when a mentor has previous experience working in that school
note: Also finds higher reading and math achievement with more mentoring hours.

correct_citation: Jennings, P. A., Brown, J. L., Frank, J. L., et al. (2017). Impacts of the CARE for Teachers program on teachers' social and emotional competence and classroom interactions. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(7), 1010-1028. ERIC ED641497 (online first).
design: Cluster randomized trial, 36 urban elementary schools, 224 teachers; wait-list control
population_location: New York City elementary schools
outcome: Teacher self-reports (emotion regulation, mindfulness, psychological distress, time urgency, etc.) and CLASS observations; teacher absences/attendance not measured
effect_as_reported: Significant positive effects on adaptive emotion regulation, mindfulness, psychological distress (reduced) and time urgency, and on CLASS emotional support
excerpt: Analyses showed that CARE for Teachers had statistically significant direct positive effects on adaptive emotion regulation, mindfulness, psychological distress, and time urgency.
note: No teacher absence or attendance outcome found in the full text ("absent" appears only for missed training sessions).

correct_citation: Ehrenberg, R. G., Ehrenberg, R. A., Rees, D. I., & Ehrenberg, E. L. (1991). School district leave policies, teacher absenteeism, and student achievement. Journal of Human Resources, 26(1), 72-105 (NBER WP 2874, 1989). ERIC EJ420928.
design: Econometric cross-district analysis of over 700 New York State districts in 1986-87
population_location: New York State school districts (excluding NYC)
outcome: Teacher leave usage; student pass rates on standardized tests
effect_as_reported: Leave policies influence leave use; student absenteeism associated with lower pass rates; teacher absence for the most part not associated with pass rates
excerpt: In contrast, teacher absence from the classroom, at least at the levels currently observed in New York State, for the most part does not appear to be associated with students' pass rates on these tests.
note: Findings confirmed. Design is a single-year (1986-87) cross-section of districts in the WP, not a panel.

correct_citation: Richard, E. D., Walter, R. A., & Yoder, E. P. (2013). The effect of capstone cooperative education experiences, and related factors, on career and technical education secondary student summative assessment scores. Career and Technical Education Research, 38(1), 19-37. doi:10.5328/cter38.1.19. ERIC EJ1033602.
design: Observational baseline comparison of co-op participants vs non-participants
population_location: Pennsylvania secondary CTE students
outcome: NOCTI summative assessment scores
effect_as_reported: Co-op participants scored significantly higher; GPA, IEP status, co-op length and Training Plan quality did not account for the differences
excerpt: students who participated in capstone cooperative education experiences scored significantly higher on summative assessments, as measured by NOCTI scores, than those students who did not participate.
note: Wrong journal: published in Career and Technical Education Research 38(1), not the Journal of STEM Teacher Education. Substance is supported; the specific controls used could not be read beyond the abstract.

correct_citation: Staklis, S., & Klein, S. (2010). Technical skill attainment and post-program outcomes: An analysis of Pennsylvania secondary career and technical education graduates. NRCCTE / MPR Associates. ERIC ED521333.
design: Logistic regression on merged statewide records controlling for race/ethnicity, gender, advanced math/science courses and GPA (enrollment); bivariate tests of association for employment
population_location: Over 21,500 Pennsylvania CTE concentrator graduates with NOCTI scores, 2005-06 and 2006-07
outcome: Postsecondary enrollment (NSC); self-reported employment (PDE follow-up survey)
effect_as_reported: Odds of enrolling 1.39 times higher (occupation-specific, highest vs lowest level) and 2.22 times higher (workplace readiness); certifications not significantly related to enrollment; skill level positively associated with employment for occupation-specific assessments only
excerpt: the odds of CTE program graduates enrolling in higher education are greater by a factor of 1.39 for those with the highest level of technical skill than those with the lowest level
note: Regression with controls covers postsecondary enrollment only; employment was examined with bivariate tests of association, using a low-response survey (about 29% matched).

correct_citation: Glennie, E., Dalton, B., Studley, R., & Lauff, E. (2025). The influence of earning industry certifications on high school graduation: Evidence from Florida. Educational Policy. doi:10.1177/08959048241292625. ERIC EJ1476967.
design: Quasi-experimental design (specific method not stated in abstract)
population_location: Florida high school students
outcome: On-time high school graduation
effect_as_reported: Certifications exert a meaningful influence on graduation likelihood, stronger for students at risk of dropping out or economically disadvantaged; no magnitude in abstract
excerpt: Our findings indicate that certifications exert a meaningful influence on the likelihood of high school graduation, and that the effect is stronger for students who are at risk for dropping out or are economically disadvantaged.
note: Direction and subgroup pattern confirmed from the abstract. The full text (Sage) was blocked, so the specific QED method and the effect size were not confirmed. The abstract also calls it an "association".

correct_citation: Lenard, M. (2023). The impacts of high school industry certifications on intentions, college-going, and earnings. SREE conference abstract. ERIC ED659423.
design: Regression discontinuity on the certification exam passing score (conditional on first attempts)
population_location: High school students taking industry-recognized certification exams (location not given in abstract)
outcome: Post-high-school intentions, postsecondary enrollment, earnings
effect_as_reported: Earners more likely to intend four-year college and just as likely to enroll; no higher earnings within seven years
excerpt: IRC earners are more likely to express their intent to attend a four-year-college and are just as likely to actually enroll
note: Abstract says effects on intentions operate through college-readiness indicators.

correct_citation: Maxwell, N., Bellotti, J., Schochet, P., Burkander, P., Whitesell, E., Dillon, E., Inanc, H., Geckeler, C., & Gonzalez, R. (2019). Building College and Career Pathways for High School Students: Youth CareerConnect. Impact Findings Report. Mathematica / U.S. Department of Labor. ERIC ED618302; WWC study 90317.
design: QED in 16 districts (6,207 YCC vs 109,541 comparison students) plus RCT in four districts; WWC reviewed the RCT (meets standards without reservations)
population_location: High school students in YCC grantee districts (31,019 participants in 130 high schools, 18 states and Puerto Rico)
outcome: School attendance, credits, ELA proficiency (QED records); RCT survey outcomes incl. earned a degree, license or certificate for work
effect_as_reported: Attendance +0.7 percentage points (90.7 to 91.5; ES 0.05) in the QED; RCT credential outcome 26.9% vs 28.9%, not significant (WWC)
excerpt: Our primary analysis found that it increased school attendance by 0.7 percentage points (from about 90.7 to 91.5 percent)
note: Credential null and attendance figures confirmed, but the attendance gain comes from the QED, not the RCT (the RCT survey attendance measures were null). WWC g = -0.06 not shown on the WWC page (improvement index not reported).

correct_citation: Miller, C., Millenky, M., Schwartz, L., Goble, L., & Stein, J. (2016). Building a Future: Interim Impact Findings from the YouthBuild Evaluation. MDRC. ERIC ED571142; WWC study 87321.
design: RCT, 75 programs, nearly 4,000 young people (3,929); WWC: meets standards without reservations
population_location: Low-income youth ages 16-24 who did not complete high school; U.S.
outcome: Earned license or certificate for work (30-month survey); high school diploma or GED
effect_as_reported: Licence/certificate 4.1% vs 2.1%, significant (WWC improvement index +16); diploma or GED 49.3% vs 36.7%, significant
excerpt: While few young people received trade licenses or training certificates (fewer than 5 percent of both groups), there was a statistically significant difference between the two groups, with the program group about 2 percentage points more likely
note: Design, population, significance and self-report (survey sample) confirmed. g = 0.42 is not printed on the WWC page; index +16 is consistent with it. Base rates are under 5%.

correct_citation: Castellano, M., Sundell, K. E., Overman, L. T., Richardson, G. B., & Stone, J. R., III (2014). Rigorous Tests of Student Outcomes in CTE Programs of Study: Final Report. NRCCTE. ERIC ED574506.
design: Multi-method longitudinal quasi-experimental design; instrumental variable approach plus post hoc regressions
population_location: 6,638 students in three urban districts in three states
outcome: Graduation, GPA, technical measures, STEM/AP credits, credential earning
effect_as_reported: POS students outperformed others on technical measures at little to no cost to academic achievement; earning industry-recognized credentials was low
excerpt: POS students outperformed other students on technical measures at little to no cost to overall academic achievement.
note: Causal (IV) graduation effect only in the first district.
